title: Quantum Numbers — Origins and Subshell Metrics
notes: Where the quantum numbers come from mathematically and the counting metrics (orbitals, capacities, designations) in one table.

• n, l and m arise as **separation constants** when the Schrödinger equation for the hydrogen atom is solved in spherical coordinates — the radial equation gives n, the angular equations give l and m. They are not assumptions; they are forced by the boundary conditions.

• mₛ does **not** come from the Schrödinger equation: it enters through the relativistic Dirac equation (1928) and was inferred earlier (1925, Uhlenbeck–Goudsmit) from the Stern–Gerlach experiment and spectral doublets.

Shell n: orbitals n², electrons 2n² (K 1/2, L 4/8, M 9/18, N 16/32). Subshell l: orbitals 2l + 1 (s 1, p 3, d 5, f 7), electrons 2(2l + 1) (s 2, p 6, d 10, f 14). Nodes: radial n − l − 1, angular l, total n − 1. Orbital designation nl (1s, 2p, 3d, 4f).

For hydrogen all subshells of a shell are degenerate (E depends only on n). In multi-electron atoms penetration makes $E_{ns}<E_{np}<E_{nd}<E_{nf}$, and across shells the (n + l) Madelung order governs filling — the two facts the Bohr–Bury scheme could not express.
• Orbitals with n = 3 → 9 = 3² (1 s + 3 p + 5 d).
• Electrons with n = 3 and m = 0 → 6 (one each in 3s, 3p, 3d, doubled by spin).
• Unpaired electrons in a subshell from Hund's rule → paramagnetism; fully paired → diamagnetism.
confusion: ❌ mₛ comes from solving the Schrödinger equation. ✅ Only n, l, m do; spin needs the Dirac equation.
❌ 2n² counts orbitals. ✅ It counts electrons; orbitals in a shell number n².
❌ All subshells of a shell have equal energy in every atom. ✅ True only for hydrogen; multi-electron atoms order them by penetration.

summary: The quantum numbers are mathematical consequences, not postulates: n, l and m appear as separation constants when the Schrödinger equation for hydrogen is solved in spherical coordinates, forced by the boundary conditions, while mₛ does not come from that equation at all — it enters through Dirac's relativistic equation (1928) and was inferred earlier (1925, Uhlenbeck and Goudsmit) from the Stern–Gerlach experiment and spectral doublets. The metrics follow immediately: a shell of principal quantum number n has n² orbitals and 2n² electrons (K 1/2, L 4/8, M 9/18, N 16/32), a subshell of quantum number l has 2l + 1 orbitals and 2(2l + 1) electrons (s 1/2, p 3/6, d 5/10, f 7/14), and the nodes are radial = n − l − 1, angular = l, total = n − 1. For hydrogen all subshells of a shell are degenerate, but in multi-electron atoms penetration gives ns < np < nd < nf and the (n + l) Madelung order governs filling across shells.
importantConcepts: n, l and m arise as separation constants of the Schrödinger equation in spherical coordinates, forced by boundary conditions
mₛ does not come from Schrödinger; it enters through Dirac's equation and the Stern–Gerlach/doublet evidence
Shell metrics: orbitals n² and electrons 2n² — K 1/2, L 4/8, M 9/18, N 16/32
Subshell metrics: orbitals 2l + 1 and electrons 2(2l + 1) — s 1/2, p 3/6, d 5/10, f 7/14
Energy order: degenerate in hydrogen, but ns < np < nd < nf by penetration, with (n + l) governing filling across shells
importantStatements: 2n² counts electrons in a shell; the number of orbitals in that shell is n².
Only n, l and m come from the Schrödinger solution — attributing spin to it is a standard error.
The Stern–Gerlach experiment (1922) split a silver beam into two, the first evidence for spin.
For hydrogen the n = 2 level is degenerate across 2s and three 2p orbitals, four states in all.
The 4f subshell (l = 3) holds 14 electrons, the width of the lanthanide series.

keyPoints: Three counting numbers to memorise: 2l + 1 orbitals, 2(2l + 1) subshell electrons, 2n² shell electrons.
Attribute spin to Dirac and Stern–Gerlach, never to Schrödinger alone.
n = 4 gives 16 orbitals and 32 electrons, made up of 4s, 4p, 4d, 4f.
Degeneracy holds only for one-electron atoms.
specialNotes: Electrons with n = 4 and l = 2 means the 4d subshell, so 2(2·2 + 1) = 10 electrons.
The energy order of subshells changes with Z, inside ions and in ligand fields, so no single order is absolute.
Spin–orbit coupling needs the total angular momentum J, beyond the four numbers treated here.
examShortTricks: Orbitals in a shell = n²; electrons in a shell = 2n² — keep the two apart.
Electrons with given n and m: count the subshells that contain an orbital with that m and double it.
4f = 7 orbitals, 14 electrons — the lanthanide series width.
